summary: This experimental RFC specifies Intent-Driven Service Mapping: BGP expresses intent-based association of overlay routes with underlay routes having specific traffic engineering characteristics that meet an SLA.

eli5.summary: Customers can ask for fast lanes or cheap lanes, and BGP matches each to the right road.

subtitle: Let customers pick fast lanes or cheap lanes, and BGP matches services to the right paths

tldr.problem: Large networks offer different service levels (low-latency, high-bandwidth, best-effort) but have no standard way to align customer requests with the right underlying tunnels across multiple domains. Existing approaches require complex configuration or MPLS everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Transport Classes to group tunnels with similar characteristics, and uses BGP to advertise which Transport Class each tunnel belongs to. Services can request a specific Transport Class using a Mapping Community (like a color tag), and BGP automatically resolves that request to the right tunnel, with fallback options.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now enforce Service Level Agreements transparently. A customer requesting a low-latency path automatically gets routed through low-latency tunnels. If those are unavailable, traffic falls back to best-effort. This works both within one network and across multiple provider networks.

today: RFC 9832 is an Experimental specification that invites implementation and deployment to test the applicability of BGP Classful Transport to real networks. The document explicitly supports the Network Slicing framework defined in RFC 9543, offering a standards-based mechanism for realizing network slices with distinct SLAs. Feedback from operational networks is expected to determine whether BGP CT advances to the Standards Track.

sections.title: Intent-Driven Routing
sections.content:
Provider networks carry many types of traffic, each with different requirements. Some services need low latency (video calls, trading), some need high bandwidth (backups), and others just need basic connectivity. Traditionally, the network has one set of paths, and services cannot express what they need.

This RFC introduces Intent-Driven Service Mapping: customers and services attach a label (called a Mapping Community, often a 'Color') to indicate their desired Service Level Agreement (SLA). The network then automatically routes that service through tunnels that meet that SLA. For example, a service marked with Color 100 (gold/low-latency) will use a low-latency tunnel; one marked Color 200 (bronze/best-effort) will use a regular tunnel. If the preferred tunnel is down, the service can fall back to the next option.
sections.eli5: Instead of routers picking routes by themselves, customers can say what kind of service they want. The network looks up tunnels that match and uses those. If the first choice fails, it uses a backup tunnel.

sections.title: Transport Classes and Tunnel Groups
sections.content:
The core concept is the Transport Class (TC): a group of tunnels that offer similar traffic engineering characteristics. For example, all low-latency tunnels (those avoiding congested links, or with latency SLA guarantees) form one Transport Class. All best-effort tunnels form another.

A Transport Class is identified by a Transport Class ID, a 32-bit number. The operator assigns these numbers consistently across the network. For example:

  • Transport Class ID 100 = Gold (low-latency)
  • Transport Class ID 200 = Silver (high-bandwidth)
  • Transport Class ID 0 = Best-Effort (default fallback)

Each Transport Class has an associated Transport Route Database (TRDB), which is a logical collection of tunnel routes belonging to that class. When a service wants to use a specific Transport Class, it looks up the destination in that class's TRDB and finds a tunnel to use. If no tunnel is found in the primary class, the service can check a backup class (also defined in the TRDB list).

Tunnels are placed into a Transport Class based on their characteristics: an operator might classify RSVP-TE tunnels with low-latency parameters into the Gold class, and simple best-effort tunnels into the Best-Effort class.
sections.eli5: All the fast roads are grouped as Gold. All the regular roads are Best-Effort. Each group has a number (ID) that routers use to keep them organized.

sections.title: Resolution Schemes and Mapping Communities
sections.content:
A Resolution Scheme is an ordered list of TRDBs that a router uses when resolving a service request. For example:

  • Scheme for Color 100: Try Gold TRDB, then fall back to Best-Effort TRDB
  • Scheme for Color 200: Try Silver TRDB, then fall back to Best-Effort TRDB
  • Scheme with no color: Use Best-Effort TRDB

A Mapping Community is a label on a service route (such as an IP prefix or BGP route) that indicates which Resolution Scheme to use. Common examples are:

  • Color Extended Community: a well-known community like color:0:100 (meaning use the scheme for Color 100)
  • Transport Class Route Target: a special community that identifies a Transport Class directly

When a router receives a service route with a Mapping Community, it looks up that community in its locally configured Resolution Schemes. It then tries to resolve the route's destination address using the TRDBs in order. If it finds a tunnel in the primary TRDB, the route is resolved over that tunnel. If not, it tries the next TRDB in the list. This automatic fallback is key to making Intent-Driven routing robust.
sections.eli5: A service says color:0:100 (I want Gold). The router says: OK, I will try the Gold road, and if that is broken, I will use the Regular road. The service does not know or care about the fallback—it just gets there.

sections.title: BGP Classful Transport Address Family
sections.content:
To advertise Transport Classes across domain boundaries, the RFC defines a new BGP address family called BGP Classful Transport (BGP CT). It uses AFI/SAFI 1/76 for IPv4 and 2/76 for IPv6.

BGP CT routes carry transport prefixes (tunnel endpoints) in the NLRI, along with:

  • RD:EP (Route Distinguisher and Endpoint): the tunnel's endpoint address, with a Route Distinguisher for uniqueness
  • Transport Class Route Target: a new extended community identifying which Transport Class the tunnel belongs to
  • MPLS Label: (when readvertising to adjacent domains) a label used to forward traffic through the tunnel

When a border node receives a BGP CT route, it:

  1. Uses the Transport Class Route Target to determine which TRDB to place the route in
  2. Installs the route in that TRDB
  3. If readvertising to adjacent domains, allocates a new MPLS label and advertises the route with that label

This design allows tunnels to be extended transparently across domain boundaries without requiring each tunnel to have its own loopback address or per-color infrastructure.
sections.eli5: BGP now carries information about tunnels and what Transport Class they belong to. Border routers read this information, put tunnels in the right groups, and pass the information to the next domain, adding labels as needed.

sections.title: End-to-End Path Setup
sections.content:
The procedures for setting up Intent-aware paths are:

Step 1: Configure Transport Classes. Operators define Transport Classes on each Service Node (SN) and Border Node (BN) in their domain, assigning each class an ID and Route Target.

Step 2: Classify and advertise tunnels. Tunneling protocols (RSVP-TE, SR-TE, or others) place their tunnels into Transport Classes based on the tunnel's TE characteristics. When a tunnel is placed in a Transport Class, its endpoint is advertised in BGP CT with the corresponding Transport Class Route Target.

Step 3: Service routes request Intent via Mapping Community. Egress SNs/PEs advertise service routes (IP prefixes) with a Mapping Community (e.g., color:0:100). This signals the desired SLA.

Step 4: Ingress nodes resolve using Resolution Schemes. When an ingress SN/PE receives the service route, it looks up the Mapping Community and finds the corresponding Resolution Scheme. It then resolves the route's next-hop address using the ordered list of TRDBs in that scheme. The resolved tunnel is used for forwarding.

Step 5: Border nodes extend tunnels across domains. When a border node receives a BGP CT tunnel route from an adjacent domain, it installs it in the appropriate TRDB and readvertises it with next-hop self and a new MPLS label. This extends the tunnel to adjacent domains.

The result is an end-to-end Intent-aware path from ingress to egress, spanning potentially multiple domains and tunneling technologies, all coordinated transparently via BGP and Transport Classes.
sections.eli5: Operators set up the path. Tunnels get labels saying what class they belong to. Services ask for a class. Routers look up tunnels of that class and use them. If a tunnel crosses into another domain, the border router keeps the path going and tells the next domain what class it is.

sections.title: Network Slicing and Multi-Domain Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC describes applicability to Network Slicing (RFC 9543), where a network operator creates virtual network instances with distinct SLAs for different customers or services. Each slice can be realized using a set of Transport Classes.

The procedures work equally for intra-AS deployments (within a single operator's network), inter-AS option A (dedicated connections between domains), inter-AS option B (shared infrastructure), and inter-AS option C (direct EBGP adjacency). This broad applicability makes BGP CT useful for both simple networks and complex multi-provider environments.

The RFC also notes that BGP CT can be used alongside IPv6, Segment Routing (SR), and Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6). In each case, the underlay tunnels are classified into Transport Classes, and the procedures for Intent-driven routing remain the same.

Backward compatibility is ensured: services without a Mapping Community default to the Best-Effort Transport Class, so they continue to work even in networks that do not yet support BGP CT.
sections.eli5: The system works for all kinds of network layouts: one domain, two domains, or many domains. It also works with different tunnel technologies as long as they all agree on Transport Class IDs. Old services that do not ask for a specific class just use the regular path.

items.title: Gold (TC ID 100)
items.text: Low-latency tunnels, avoids congested links, strict SLA

items.title: Silver (TC ID 200)
items.text: High-bandwidth tunnels, optimized for bulk transfer

items.title: Best-Effort (TC ID 0)
items.text: Regular tunnels, no SLA, used as fallback

left.title: BGP LU (AFI/SAFI 1/4)
left.desc: Carries one tunnel endpoint per loopback. Requires multiple loopback IPs to distinguish different SLAs.

right.title: BGP CT (AFI/SAFI 1/76)
right.desc: Carries tunnel endpoint with Transport Class RT, distinguishing SLAs without multiple loopbacks. Scales better.
